arXiv:2605.02568v1 [cs.LG] 04 May 2026

StreamIndex: Memory-Bounded Compressed Sparse Attention via Streaming Top-k

Jaber Jaber ††thanks: Correspondence: jaber@rightnowai.co Affiliation: RightNow AI Email: jaber@rightnowai.co    Osama Jaber Affiliation: RightNow AI Email: osama@rightnowai.co
Abstract

DeepSeek-V3.2 and V4 introduce Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA): a lightning indexer (a learned scoring projection over compressed keys) scores them, the top-kk are selected per query, and a sparse attention kernel reads only those. Public CSA implementations materialize a [B,S,HI,T][B,S,H_{I},T] FP32 score tensor before the top-kk reduction. With HI=64H_{I}{=}64 indexer heads and the V4-Flash compression ratio m=4m{=}4, that intermediate is 256 GB at sequence length S=65,536S{=}65{,}536, exceeding any single-GPU high-bandwidth-memory (HBM) budget. We present StreamIndex, a Triton implementation of the CSA pipeline whose central component is a chunked partition-merge top-kk driver that never materializes the full intermediate. On synthetic-but-realistic V4-shaped inputs at the indexer-step (layer) level on a single NVIDIA H200, the materialize path runs out of memory (OOMs) at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536 with V4-Flash dimensions; StreamIndex runs the same indexer to S=1,048,576S{=}1{,}048{,}576 with 6.21 GB peak HBM, a 32×\times regime extension. Set-overlap recall against the materialize ground truth is bit-exact at small SS where both fit; across three 5-point design-space sweeps (chunk size, key-tile size, top-kk), mean recall rounds to 1.0000 with min recall at least 0.9980 in every cell. The chunked driver composes with TileLang’s pipelined attention kernel: at S=262,144S{=}262{,}144 with V4-Flash dimensions, the materialize indexer paired with TileLang attention OOMs while the chunked indexer paired with the same attention runs in 1.97 s at 18.56 GB peak. Our contribution targets the indexer step; we make no claim of a faster attention kernel or of real-checkpoint end-to-end behavior. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/StreamIndex.

1 Introduction

DeepSeek-V3.2 and V4 attach a learned indexer to the attention path DeepSeek-AI (2025). The indexer scores compressed keys, the top-kk are selected, and a sparse attention kernel reads only those keys for each query. The pattern preserves quality at long context while reducing the attention step from O⁡(S2)O(S^{2}) to O⁡(S⋅k)O(S\cdot k). V4-Flash and V4-Pro extend this to a 1M-token context with HI=64H_{I}{=}64 indexer heads, m=4m{=}4 key compression, and per-query top-k∈{512,1024}k\in\{512,1024\} DeepSeek-AI (2025).

The claim that CSA scales to 1M context relies on the indexer step itself fitting. The lightning-indexer score I⁡(t,s)=∑h=1HIwt,h⋅ReLU⁡(qt,h⋅Ks)I(t,s)=\sum_{h=1}^{H_{I}}w_{t,h}\cdot\mathrm{ReLU}(q_{t,h}\cdot K_{s}) is computed in the V4 reference (model.py) and in TileLang’s reference Wang et al. (2025) as a fused einsum producing the intermediate [B,S,HI,T][B,S,H_{I},T] FP32 tensor before the head sum. With V4-Flash dimensions (HI=64H_{I}{=}64, T=S/mT{=}S/m), this intermediate is 256 GB at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536 and 1 TB at S=131,072S{=}131{,}072 on a single batch. Every public CSA pipeline we are aware of OOMs on a single H200 (140 GB HBM) for S≥64S\geq 64K with V4-Flash dimensions, before the top-kk has been selected, before any attention has run.

Existing long-context attention work attacks the attention step directly: FlashAttention Dao et al. (2022); Dao (2023); Shah et al. (2024) fuses softmax with the matmul, paged attention Kwon et al. (2023) chunks the KV cache, ring attention Liu et al. (2023) sequence-parallelizes. None of these address the indexer-step intermediate that gates V4-class CSA at long context. Native Sparse Attention (NSA) Yuan et al. (2025) replaces the indexer entirely with a learned top-kk structure, but inherits a different memory profile and is not drop-in compatible with V4 checkpoints.

We attack the indexer step directly. The lightning-indexer score is per-key separable: once the query is fixed, the score is a pure function of the key index, with no inter-key coupling (no softmax, no normalization that mixes scores). This separability makes the top-kk commute with iteration order over the key axis, which is folklore in streaming algorithms Charikar et al. (2002). We apply that fact to the V4 indexer in a chunked partition-merge implementation: process queries and keys in (cS,cT)(c_{S},c_{T}) tiles, take per-tile top-kk, merge across tiles. Peak HBM for the score buffer drops from O⁡(B⋅S⋅HI⋅T)O(B\cdot S\cdot H_{I}\cdot T) to O⁡(B⋅cS⋅cT)O(B\cdot c_{S}\cdot c_{T}).

Key insight.

The indexer step is what gates CSA at long context, not the attention kernel. The attention step has streaming patterns (FlashAttention) and is well-served by existing CUDA kernels; the indexer-step intermediate is the unaddressed bottleneck. A Python-level chunked driver over a fused score kernel removes the peak-memory bottleneck while empirically matching the materialize top-kk as a set on tested parity cases.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    StreamIndex, an open-source Triton implementation of the V4 CSA pipeline whose chunked partition-merge top-kk driver realizes the streaming top-kk invariance for the lightning indexer (151 lines, chunked_indexer.py).

  2. 2.

    A per-chunk causal-mask formulation that keeps mask memory at O⁡(cS⋅cT)O(c_{S}\cdot c_{T}) instead of O⁡(S⋅T)O(S\cdot T), which is what allows the chunked path itself to scale past S=131,072S{=}131{,}072.

  3. 3.

    A measured 32×\times regime extension at V4-Flash dimensions on a single H200: the materialize indexer OOMs at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536, our chunked indexer runs at S=1,048,576S{=}1{,}048{,}576 with 6.21 GB peak HBM.

  4. 4.

    A pipeline-composition result: at S=262,144S{=}262{,}144 with V4-Flash dimensions and TileLang’s pipelined attention kernel as the common backend, the materialize-indexer path OOMs while our chunked-indexer path runs at 1.97 s, 18.56 GB peak.

  5. 5.

    A design-space and ablation study (3 sweeps, 3 ablations) showing that chunk size has a clear knee around cS=2048c_{S}{=}2048, single-chunk over TT is optimal when memory allows, and FP32 score accumulation is necessary (FP16 drops perfect-recall rows from 99.99% to 91.82%).

  6. 6.

    Bit-exact set-overlap recall versus the V4-Flash materialize-then-postmask reference at S∈{2048,4096,8192}S\in\{2048,4096,8192\}, validated under realistic post-projection input distributions.

2 Related Work

Table 1 positions StreamIndex against prior long-context attention work. Every entry except the V4 reference and StreamIndex optimizes the attention or KV-cache step. StreamIndex is the first open-source CSA implementation that does not materialize the indexer-step intermediate.

Sparse and compressed attention.

The structured-sparsity line started with Sparse Transformers Child et al. (2019), Longformer Beltagy et al. (2020), and BigBird Zaheer et al. (2020): predetermined block, dilated, or random sparsity patterns. DeepSeek-V2 DeepSeek-AI (2024a) and V3 DeepSeek-AI (2024b) introduced Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) with a low-rank KV factorization. V3.2 DeepSeek-AI (2025) adds the Compressed Sparse Attention pattern with the lightning indexer; V4-Flash and V4-Pro generalize to 1M context. Native Sparse Attention Yuan et al. (2025) learns a sparsity pattern jointly with the model. None of the public reference kernels for these methods address the indexer-step memory peak we attack.

Query-aware sparse inference.

Quest Tang et al. (2024) and MInference Jiang et al. (2024b) both compute query-dependent sparsity at inference time. Quest selects KV pages by a small score per page; MInference picks dynamic patterns per attention head. Both target the attention-step compute, not the indexer-step intermediate. Selective Attention Leviathan et al. (2024) provides a related principled mechanism. Mixture-of-experts work Jiang et al. (2024a) influences the broader V4 architecture but is orthogonal to the attention path.

IO-aware attention.

FlashAttention Dao et al. (2022); Dao (2023); Shah et al. (2024) fuses softmax with QK and PV matmuls so attention is computed without materializing the S×SS\times S score matrix. The technique applies to dense attention; in CSA it bypasses the attention-step bottleneck but leaves the indexer-step intermediate intact.

Long-context infrastructure.

PagedAttention in vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) chunks the KV cache. Ring attention Liu et al. (2023) sequence-parallelizes across devices. StreamingLLM Xiao et al. (2024) keeps a fixed window plus attention sinks. H2O Zhang et al. (2023) retains heavy hitters. Each addresses the KV-cache or attention pass; the V4 indexer’s [B,S,HI,T][B,S,H_{I},T] intermediate is orthogonal.

Approximate and structured attention.

Linformer Wang et al. (2020), Performer Choromanski et al. (2021), Reformer Kitaev et al. (2020), and linear attention Katharopoulos et al. (2020) approximate softmax attention with low-rank, locality-sensitive-hashing (LSH), or kernel structure. State-space models such as Mamba Gu and Dao (2023) and Hyena Poli et al. (2023) avoid attention entirely. CSA, which V4-Flash uses, is exact (top-kk keys are read fully); we preserve that property. Multi-query attention Shazeer (2019) and its variants reduce KV-cache size by sharing keys/values across heads; V4-Flash uses an MLA layout that is a generalization.

Streaming top-k.

Partition-merge invariance for top-kk over a separable scoring function is folklore; Charikar et al. Charikar et al. (2002) state and use it for streaming heavy-hitter problems, and the textbook treatment is in Mitzenmacher and Upfal Mitzenmacher and Upfal (2017). Our contribution is engineering: applying it to the V4 lightning indexer in the first publicly-available CSA implementation we are aware of that does not materialize the score intermediate.

Triton and tiled kernels.

Triton Tillet et al. (2019) is the kernel language we use. TileLang Wang et al. (2025) provides reference CSA kernels that we benchmark against (their attention kernel; their reference indexer materializes).

3 Background: V4 Compressed Sparse Attention

The CSA pipeline.

A V4 CSA layer takes a hidden state x∈ℝB×S×dx\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times d} and produces an attention output of the same shape. Internally:

  1. 1.

    A token compressor produces a compressed key/value cache KC∈ℝB×T×dhK_{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d_{h}} where T=S/mT=S/m (m=4m{=}4 for V4-Flash).

  2. 2.

    A lightning indexer scores each compressed key for each query: I⁡(t,s)=∑hwt,h​ReLU​(qt,h⋅KCs)I(t,s)=\sum_{h}w_{t,h}\mathrm{ReLU}(q_{t,h}\cdot K_{C}^{s}) for h∈[HI]h\in[H_{I}], s∈[T]s\in[T], t∈[S]t\in[S].

  3. 3.

    For each query tt, the indexer selects TopK⁡(t)\mathrm{TopK}(t), the indices of the top-kk legal compressed keys.

  4. 4.

    A sparse attention kernel reads only TopK⁡(t)∪Window⁡(t)\mathrm{TopK}(t)\cup\mathrm{Window}(t) for each query and returns the attention output.

The indexer-step intermediate.

The reference V4-Flash forward (references/DeepSeek-V4-Flash/inference/model.py, lines 415–423) computes the indexer score as

⬇
index_score = torch.einsum("bshd,btd->bsht", q, kv_cache_slice)
index_score = (index_score.relu_() * weights.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(dim=2)

The first line produces a [B,S,HI,T][B,S,H_{I},T] FP32 tensor; the second reduces over HIH_{I}. With V4-Flash dimensions (B=1B{=}1, HI=64H_{I}{=}64, T=S/4T{=}S/4), this intermediate is 256256 GB at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536 and 4 TB at S=262,144S{=}262{,}144.

This is the bottleneck. The downstream attention kernel does not see it. The Triton-based or TileLang-based attention kernel that comes after has access only to the compact top-kk index list. The score intermediate is allocated and freed inside the indexer step alone, which means the indexer step gates the maximum sequence length the pipeline can run, regardless of how efficient the attention kernel is. Assuming attention is the bottleneck at long context is incorrect for CSA: the pipeline runs out of memory in the indexer step before attention runs.

Per-element variance.

The lightning-indexer score is well-conditioned at training scale: qq is rotary-position-embedded Su et al. (2024), Hadamard-rotated Ashkboos et al. (2024), and quantized to FP4 Rouhani et al. (2023), so qt,h⋅KCsq_{t,h}\cdot K_{C}^{s} has approximately unit variance per element. Weights wt,hw_{t,h} are unconstrained-sign output of a trained linear projection. We use these distributional facts to construct synthetic but spec-matched inputs for the parity tests in §6.

4 Streaming Top-k for the Lightning Indexer

4.1 Total order on (score, index) pairs

Top-kk requires a tie-breaking rule. We define ≻\succ on ℝ×ℤ≥0\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} by

(a,i)≻(b,j)⟺a>b∨(a=b∧i<j).(a,i)\succ(b,j)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a>b\;\lor\;(a=b\;\land\;i<j).

This is a strict total order. Ties on score are broken in favor of the smaller index, matching the inductive bias of causal language modeling. PyTorch’s torch.topk does not guarantee any tie-break, so set comparison (not index-position comparison) is the right notion of equivalence.

4.2 Effective top-k

Causal masking restricts the legal index range. Let Tlegal​(t)=⌊(t+1)/m⌋T_{\mathrm{legal}}(t)=\lfloor(t+1)/m\rfloor be the number of compressed blocks fully inside the past of query tt. The output size is keff​(t)=min⁡(k,Tlegal​(t))k_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)=\min(k,T_{\mathrm{legal}}(t)), padded to kk with the sentinel value −1-1 when Tlegal​(t)<kT_{\mathrm{legal}}(t)<k.

4.3 The partition-merge invariance

Theorem (partition-merge invariance, idealized deterministic top-kk).

Algorithm 1 returns the unordered set of the top-min⁡(k,Tlegal)\min(k,T_{\mathrm{legal}}) pairs under ≻\succ, regardless of the permutation chosen in the loop. We write this set as argtop≻k​g\mathrm{argtop}_{\succ}^{k}g. Sentinel padding (used when Tlegal<kT_{\mathrm{legal}}<k) is post-processing and is excluded from set comparisons.

Proof sketch. Strong induction on prefix length jj. Let MjM_{j} be the top-kk of the first jj processed pairs under ≻\succ, and HjH_{j} the heap state after step jj. The base case j=0j{=}0 gives M0=H0=∅M_{0}=H_{0}=\emptyset. The inductive step splits on whether j+1≤kj{+}1\leq k (every element survives) or j+1>kj{+}1>k. In the latter case, the new element either is ≻\succ-greater than Hj.peek⁡()H_{j}.\mathrm{peek}() (it displaces the ≻\succ-min, preserving top-kk) or not (it does not enter Mj+1M_{j+1}, again preserving top-kk). In all cases Hj+1=Mj+1H_{j+1}=M_{j+1}. The full proof, with the tied-score case, is in the source repository at docs/streaming_topk.md. □\square

Implementation note (set parity, not order parity).

The strict total order ≻\succ is defined for the formal theorem statement, but our implementation uses torch.topk on raw FP32 scores, whose tie-breaking is unspecified. We therefore do not derive set-parity from the ≻\succ-theorem; we empirically verify (§6) bit-exact set match between the materialize and chunked top-kk outputs. On all parity tests at V4-Flash dimensions the two paths agree on the set, including under FP32 tied-score conditions. This empirical guarantee matches the practical use of the indexer, which feeds the index set to the attention kernel where order is irrelevant; promoting it to a derived corollary would require inlining a deterministic comparator in both paths, which neither the materialize reference nor our implementation does.

Corollary (chunked partition-merge).

For any partition [Tlegal]=P1⊔P2⊔⋯⊔Pn[T_{\mathrm{legal}}]=P_{1}\sqcup P_{2}\sqcup\dots\sqcup P_{n},

argtop≻k​g=topk≻​(⋃i=1nargtop≻min⁡(k,|Pi|)​g|Pi).\mathrm{argtop}^{k}_{\succ}g=\mathrm{topk}_{\succ}\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{argtop}^{\min(k,|P_{i}|)}_{\succ}g|_{P_{i}}\Bigr).

This is what enables chunked execution: process partitions independently, take per-partition top-kk, merge.

5 The Chunked Indexer

StreamIndex instantiates the corollary of §4 as a Python driver over Triton primitives. Figure 1 shows the data flow.

Fused score kernel (indexer_score.py, 198 lines).

A single autotuned Triton kernel computes scoreb,t,s=∑hwb,t,h⋅ReLU⁡(qb,t,h,d⋅KC​b,s,d)\mathrm{score}_{b,t,s}=\sum_{h}w_{b,t,h}\cdot\mathrm{ReLU}(q_{b,t,h,d}\cdot K_{C\,b,s,d}) on a [cS,cT][c_{S},c_{T}] tile. The tensor of head-wise scores is reduced to [cS,cT][c_{S},c_{T}] FP32 inside the kernel before any global memory write; we never materialize the HIH_{I}-axis intermediate. This is the unit of work the chunked driver issues per tile.

Chunked driver (chunked_indexer.py, 151 lines).

The driver is the body of Algorithm 2. It maintains a running top-kk buffer per query, indexed by the outer SS-tile. For each TT-tile, it calls the fused score kernel, applies the per-tile causal mask (§5), takes per-tile top-kk, and merges into the running buffer.

Per-chunk causal mask.

A naive implementation passes a [B,S,T][B,S,T] bool causal mask. At S=131,072S{=}131{,}072, T=32,768T{=}32{,}768 that mask is 4 GB; at S=1S{=}1M, T=256T{=}256K it is 256 GB. We add an integer parameter causal_ratio to the chunked driver: the mask t<⌊(s+1)/m⌋t<\lfloor(s+1)/m\rfloor is constructed per (cS,cT)(c_{S},c_{T}) tile from torch.arange on the appropriate offsets. Per-tile mask memory is O⁡(cS⋅cT)O(c_{S}\cdot c_{T}), independent of SS and TT. This single change is what allows the chunked path itself to scale past S=131,072S{=}131{,}072.

Auto-detection.

The end-to-end CSA forward (flash_sparse/csa.py, 199 lines) selects the materialize path when the would-be score matrix fits in 1 GB and the chunked path otherwise. Small-SS workloads stay on the materialize path, which is faster when it fits (no merge overhead).

6 Experimental Evaluation

We measure StreamIndex’s chunked indexer (§5) along five axes: bit-exact parity at small SS, layer-level scaling and the OOM threshold (§6.2), V4-Pro dimensions, full-pipeline composition with TileLang attention, and design-space sweeps and ablations.

Hardware and methodology.

All runs are on a single NVIDIA H200 SXM with 140 GB HBM3e, BF16 precision, CUDA 13, Triton 3.7, PyTorch 2.13 nightly. Timings use torch.cuda.Event with at least 1 warmup and 3 measured iterations after autotune. Peak HBM is measured with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated, with baseline subtracted after a separate warmup pass so JIT compilation is excluded.

Synthetic-but-realistic inputs.

Where the V4-Flash modelling-code projections cannot be loaded (no checkpoint on a single H200 fits the 270 GB FP8 Micikevicius et al. (2022) V4-Flash weights), we draw q,KC∼𝒩⁡(0,1/dh)q,K_{C}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/d_{h}) to match per-element variance after the wq_b →\to unflatten →\to RoPE Su et al. (2024) →\to Hadamard Ashkboos et al. (2024) →\to FP4 Rouhani et al. (2023) pipeline, and use a freshly-initialized nn.Linear(d,HId,H_{I}) for the weights projection scaled by 1dh⋅HI\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{h}\cdot H_{I}}} to match the V4 reference. We label all numerical results in this section as “synthetic-but-realistic.”

6.1 Bit-exact parity at small SS

We replicate the V4-Flash Indexer.forward materialize+topk+postmask code path verbatim and compare its output to our chunked-indexer output via per-query set-overlap recall over valid (non-pad) entries, with a strict gate (mean == min == 1.0).

Table 2 reports 100% mean and min recall on every tested row. The chunked indexer is bit-exact on this workload.

6.2 Layer-level scaling: 32×\times regime extension

Table 3 is the headline result; Figure 2 plots both axes. The materialize indexer OOMs at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536: the [B,S,HI,T][B,S,H_{I},T] FP32 intermediate is 256 GB at this size, exceeding the 140 GB HBM of an H200. The chunked indexer runs to S=1,048,576S{=}1{,}048{,}576 with 6.21 GB peak. The runnable-SS regime extends from 32K (where materialize uses 129/140 GB) to 1M (chunked, 6.21/140 GB) — a 32×\times extension on a single H200.

At S=32S{=}32K where both fit, the chunked path is also faster (10.3×\times). This is because the materialize path produces a 64 GB intermediate before the head-sum, then a separate 1 GB intermediate after. The Triton score kernel does the head-sum inline and never allocates the large intermediate, so even when memory is not the binding constraint the chunked path wins on memory-traffic.

6.3 V4-Pro dimensions

The V4-Pro indexer step (Table 4) shows the same OOM threshold at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536 for materialize and the same 1M chunked ceiling. The peak HBM is roughly 2×2\times that of V4-Flash because k=1024k{=}1024 doubles the running-buffer allocations.

6.4 Pipeline composition with TileLang attention

The chunked indexer is one component of a CSA forward; it must compose cleanly with whichever attention kernel runs downstream. We test composition with TileLang’s pipelined sparse attention kernel Wang et al. (2025), the production-quality CUDA reference for V4 attention.

Table 5 confirms the result is not specific to our attention kernel. With TileLang’s CUDA attention as the backend, the materialize indexer paired with TileLang attention OOMs at S=262,144S{=}262{,}144 on an H200; the chunked indexer paired with the same TileLang attention runs in 1.97 s. The chunked indexer adds 10–15% wall-clock overhead at SS where the materialize path also runs, in exchange for SS scaling past the materialize OOM point (we measured to S=1,048,576S{=}1{,}048{,}576) and a 1.83×\times lower peak HBM at S=131,072S{=}131{,}072.

6.5 Design-space sweep

Table 6 reports three sweeps. Across all 15 cells the mean set-overlap recall rounds to 1.0000; min recall is at least 0.9980 in every cell.

The cSc_{S} sweep shows a flat time floor (about 4 s) at cS≥4096c_{S}\geq 4096 with peak HBM growing linearly. Below cS=1024c_{S}{=}1024, Python launch overhead dominates and time rises.

The cTc_{T} sweep is the most actionable finding (Figure 3): larger cTc_{T} is monotonically faster across the measured range on H200, and the fastest configuration is a single TT-tile per SS-tile (i.e., cT=Tc_{T}=T). Per-tile launch overhead and the merge step both scale with the tile count, while the per-tile compute is well-amortized across HBM bandwidth at any cTc_{T} above 4K. The right rule for picking chunk size is: set cTc_{T} as large as fits in the cS⋅cT⋅4c_{S}\cdot c_{T}\cdot 4 bytes budget, then pick cSc_{S} to control the score-tile size.

The kk sweep is roughly linear in HBM and weakly sublinear in time across k∈{64,256,512,1024,2048}k\in\{64,256,512,1024,2048\}. The persistent output buffer (top-kk indices and scores) accounts for most of the HBM growth.

6.6 Ablations

Table 7 reports three ablations against the production path.

A2 (skip saturated chunks) sets cT=256<k=512c_{T}{=}256<k{=}512 and skips chunks rather than including all entries (the production behaviour). Recall drops to 0.02%. The production path’s branch that includes all entries when cT<kc_{T}<k is essential: those small-TT tiles contain top-kk entries that materialize would have selected.

A2 control is the same cT=256c_{T}{=}256 in the production path, recovering full mean recall (1.0000) and min recall ≥\geq 0.9980. The drop in A2 is attributable to the skip, not to the small chunk size itself.

A3 (FP16 score accumulation) casts the per-tile score and the running buffer to FP16. Mean recall stays at 0.9998 (essentially identical) but the fraction of perfect-recall rows drops from 99.99% to 91.82%: roughly 8% of rows lose a small number of entries to FP16 boundary errors. At the same cT=1024c_{T}{=}1024 multi-chunk config, the wall-clock at S=262,144S{=}262{,}144 drops to 3.52 s (1.22×\times speedup over production’s 4.31 s) and peak HBM drops to 1.07 GB (1.48×\times lower than production’s 1.58 GB). FP16 is a viable precision/throughput tradeoff in inference settings where exact top-kk is not required; FP32 is necessary for bit-exact parity with the reference.

7 Discussion and Limitations

No real-model end-to-end result (primary limitation).

We do not load V4-Flash checkpoint weights. The weights would be 270 GB at FP8 Micikevicius et al. (2022), exceeding a single H200, and weight offloading would make the run I/O-bound and uninformative for the indexer-step claim. We have not run the chunked indexer through retrieval (needle-in-a-haystack, RULER Hsieh et al. (2024)), QA (LongBench Bai et al. (2024)), or code (SWE-bench-Verified Jimenez et al. (2024)) tasks at long context, and we have not measured perplexity drift against materialize. The kernel-level evidence we present is necessary but not sufficient for a "drop-in" production claim; multi-GPU follow-up is required to close that gap. We narrow “drop-in” to mean the chunked indexer step is bit-exact at the layer level and reserve full-pipeline behavior preservation as future work.

Synthetic input distributions.

Inputs in our parity tests match per-element variance of the post-projection pipeline but not the trained-checkpoint structure. The bit-exact set-match result is an algorithmic claim (the chunked indexer is the same function as materialize+topk on the same inputs) and does not depend on input distribution; the recall-at-design-sweep finding does.

Tie-order parity is set-level, not order-level.

Our chunked driver and the materialize reference both call torch.topk, whose tie-breaking is unspecified. The partition-merge invariance is therefore only required to hold at the set level. We verify bit-exact set match against the materialize reference on every parity test (Table 2). For a strict order guarantee, the algorithm needs the lexicographic comparator ≻\succ inlined; we did not implement that because the downstream attention kernel takes the index list as a set.

The chunked driver re-reads inputs.

Total HBM I/O is the same as materialize: every q,KC,wq,K_{C},w entry is read ⌈S/cS⌉\lceil S/c_{S}\rceil or ⌈T/cT⌉\lceil T/c_{T}\rceil times, the same as the materialize einsum. Only peak is reduced. At SS where materialize fits, materialize is faster (at S=8192S{=}8192, the materialize-path pipeline composition is 6.5 ms vs the chunked-path 7.5 ms). The chunked path is the only viable option at long context, not a uniformly faster path.

Triton attention is not production-quality at dh=512d_{h}{=}512.

Our auxiliary Triton attention forward at V4-Pro dimensions reaches only 8% of the H200 BF16 peak (versus TileLang’s 40% peak with the same shape). The Triton compiler in version 3.7 does not expose the FlashAttention-3 (FA3)-style Shah et al. (2024) warp-specialization patterns needed to close that gap, which would require a CUDA reimplementation of the attention step. The contribution of this paper is on the indexer step; the attention is orthogonal and we deliberately compose with TileLang for the production-quality path.

Future work.

(i) End-to-end V4-Flash inference with weight offloading or multi-GPU tensor parallelism (TP), on retrieval (needle-in-a-haystack), QA (LongBench), and code (SWE-bench-Verified) benchmarks; (ii) a fused indexer-attention kernel sharing KCK_{C} loads across both stages; (iii) multi-hardware validation on H100, A100, and MI300X to confirm the regime extension is hardware-agnostic.

8 Conclusion

The lightning indexer in V4-class CSA gates the pipeline at long context: with HI=64H_{I}{=}64 heads and ratio m=4m{=}4, the materialize-then-topk reference path OOMs at S=65,536S{=}65{,}536 with V4-Flash dimensions on a single H200. StreamIndex ships a chunked partition-merge top-kk driver over a fused Triton score kernel that scales the same indexer step to S=1,048,576S{=}1{,}048{,}576 with 6.21 GB peak HBM, a 32×\times regime extension. The chunked driver runs unmodified with TileLang’s pipelined attention kernel and adds 10–15% wall-clock at sub-OOM SS. Bit-exact parity with the materialize path is verified at small SS. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/StreamIndex.
